The \(n_i > 50\) residual-normality bypass: scope, evidence, and boundary

Working note for the visStatistics Discussion section

2026-06-01

1 The justification of the \(n>50\) gate

For grouped numeric responses (Route 1), visstat() applies a residual normality test (Shapiro–Wilk) only when at least one group has \(n_i \le 50\). When all group sizes exceed 50, the residual-normality test is bypassed: routing proceeds straight to the variance gate and then to a mean-based test. Verified in R/visstat_core.R (all(counts_per_level > 50)). The CLT [@Lumley:2002] is the motivation for a finite cutoff, not the evidence that 50 suffices — the convergence rate of the group means to normality depends on skewness, so the cutoff is a pragmatic choice the simulations above calibrate.

The bypass fires before the homoscedasticity (Levene) gate and before the two-vs-more-groups split. At the moment it decides, it does not yet know which of four mean-based tests will run. Its justification therefore cannot rest on a single source — it must cover a 2×2 of branches.

Here is an overview of the literature regarding threshold values in the four branches:

\(k = 2\) \(k > 2\)
equal variance (Student / Fisher) Blanca et al. (2017) — Student is the two-group special case Blanca et al. (2017)
unequal variance (Welch-\(t\) / Welch-ANOVA) Fagerland (2012) Delacre et al. (2019)
  • Blanca et al. (2017) — Fisher one-way ANOVA: Type I error within Bradley’s bounds across skewness up to 2, kurtosis up to 6, group sizes 5–100, equal variances.
  • Fagerland (2012) — Welch’s \(t\), unequal variances, two groups: \(n \approx 50\) holds the 5% rate across a wide skewness range; only heavy skew needs \(\approx 200\).
  • Delacre et al. (2019) — Welch’s one-way ANOVA, unequal variances, \(k > 2\): \(\approx 50\) per group suffices, except for \(k > 4\) under pronounced skew, where \(\approx 100\) per group is needed. (page to re-verify before manuscript use.)

2 An honest test case: equal means, different medians

To probe the bypass, build \(k = 5\) lognormal groups with equal population means but unequal variance and skew. For a lognormal, \(\text{mean} = e^{\mu + \sigma^2/2}\), so fixing \(\mu_i = M - \sigma_i^2/2\) holds every group mean at \(e^{M}\) while spread and skew rise with \(\sigma_i\). Side effect: medians \(= e^{\mu_i}\) differ.

Under equal means, every rejection by a mean-based test is a false positive — it cannot be faked by a built-in mean difference.

sdlog   <- c(A = 0.3, B = 0.5, C = 0.7, D = 0.9, E = 1.1)  # rising spread/skew
M       <- 1                                               # every group mean = exp(M)
meanlog <- M - sdlog^2 / 2                                 # equalise the means

data.frame(
  group           = names(sdlog),
  pop_mean        = round(exp(meanlog + sdlog^2/2), 3),    # all equal
  pop_median      = round(exp(meanlog), 3),                # differ
  pop_sd_rank     = rank(sdlog)
)
##   group pop_mean pop_median pop_sd_rank
## A     A    2.718      2.599           1
## B     B    2.718      2.399           2
## C     C    2.718      2.128           3
## D     D    2.718      1.813           4
## E     E    2.718      1.484           5
make_data <- function(n) {
  grp <- factor(rep(names(n), times = n))
  val <- unlist(lapply(names(n), function(k) rlnorm(n[k], meanlog[k], sdlog[k])))
  list(grp = grp, val = val)
}

# pull the test visstat() actually ran (method + p) from its result object
visstat_test <- function(res) {
  for (el in res)
    if (is.list(el) && !is.null(el$method) && !is.null(el$p.value))
      return(list(method = trimws(el$method), p = el$p.value))
  list(method = "(not found)", p = NA_real_)
}

3 What visstat() does, across three size regimes

Each regime keeps the same structure; only the group sizes change. The plots are the default visstat() panels. The printed block contrasts the test visstat() chose with Kruskal–Wallis.

welch_case <- function(n, label) {
  set.seed(1)
  d   <- make_data(n)
  res <- visstat(d$grp, d$val)
  vt  <- visstat_test(res)
  kw  <- kruskal.test(d$val ~ d$grp)
  cat("===========", label, "===========\n")
  cat("means  :", paste(round(tapply(d$val, d$grp, mean),   2), collapse = " / "), "\n")
  cat("medians:", paste(round(tapply(d$val, d$grp, median), 2), collapse = " / "), "\n")
  cat(sprintf("visstat()  %-48s p = %.4g\n", vt$method, vt$p))
  cat(sprintf("Kruskal    %-48s p = %.4g\n\n", kw$method, kw$p.value))
}

welch_case(c(A = 55,  B = 65,  C = 75,  D = 85,  E = 95),  "n in (50,100)")
welch_case(c(A = 110, B = 130, C = 150, D = 170, E = 190), "n > 100")
welch_case(c(A = 510, B = 530, C = 550, D = 570, E = 590), "n > 500")
## =========== n in (50,100) ===========
## means  : 2.76 / 2.84 / 2.62 / 2.8 / 2.57 
## medians: 2.75 / 2.43 / 1.9 / 1.79 / 1.49 
## visstat()  One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances) p = 0.9097
## Kruskal    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test                     p = 9.738e-05
## 
## =========== n > 100 ===========
## means  : 2.8 / 2.64 / 2.73 / 2.95 / 2.64 
## medians: 2.72 / 2.21 / 2.19 / 1.72 / 1.22 
## visstat()  One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances) p = 0.7949
## Kruskal    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test                     p = 2.338e-11
## 
## =========== n > 500 ===========
## means  : 2.74 / 2.68 / 2.76 / 2.78 / 2.66 
## medians: 2.57 / 2.36 / 2.08 / 1.67 / 1.5 
## visstat()  One-way analysis of means (not assuming equal variances) p = 0.8875
## Kruskal    Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test                     p = 1.387e-35

Reading it: means are equal, so visstat() (Welch’s ANOVA) correctly does not reject. Medians differ, so Kruskal–Wallis correctly does. The divergence is a property of the question each test asks (mean vs. rank/location), not a bug — and it is untouched by sample size.

4 Does raising the threshold to 100 fix anything?

The single-draw view shows correctness on average. The real cost is the false-positive rate under equal means. Bradley’s liberal robustness bound for \(\alpha = .05\) is \([.025, .075]\).

welch_typeI <- function(n, nrep = 2000, alpha = 0.05) {
  grp <- factor(rep(names(n), times = n))
  set.seed(1)
  mean(replicate(nrep, {
    val <- unlist(lapply(names(n), function(k) rlnorm(n[k], meanlog[k], sdlog[k])))
    oneway.test(val ~ grp, var.equal = FALSE)$p.value < alpha
  }))
}

data.frame(
  regime       = c("n in (50,100)", "n > 100", "n > 500"),
  welch_typeI  = c(
    welch_typeI(c(A = 55,  B = 65,  C = 75,  D = 85,  E = 95)),
    welch_typeI(c(A = 110, B = 130, C = 150, D = 170, E = 190)),
    welch_typeI(c(A = 510, B = 530, C = 550, D = 570, E = 590))
  )
)
##          regime welch_typeI
## 1 n in (50,100)      0.0885
## 2       n > 100      0.0775
## 3       n > 500      0.0575

For this \(k = 5\) skewed, heteroscedastic corner: the false-positive rate is inflated at \(n \in (50,100)\), only borderline at \(n > 100\) (sitting on Bradley’s ceiling), and comfortably controlled only well past 100 per group. So a blanket “raise the cutoff to 100” does not cleanly fix it — matching Delacre et al. (2019). A single group-size threshold cannot cover the \(k > 4\) skewed-heteroscedastic corner.

5 Consequence for the package

  • Keep the bypass and the cutoff at 50: clearly supported for the cases the package targets (the 2×2 above).
  • Do not chase the corner with a \(k\)-dependent threshold: it cannot be made clean, and the bypass deliberately favours not switching to rank-based tests over negligible large-sample deviations.
  • Instead, rely on the package’s existing safeguards: every test is reported with an effect size, and the residual diagnostics are displayed, so a significant mean-based result paired with a small effect size stays visible.

6 Proposed Discussion paragraph (replaces current L898)

It also depends on which test the routing will reach. Holding the false-positive rate to its \(\alpha = 5\%\) target, simulation evidence supports the threshold of 50 across all of these branches. For equal variances—Fisher’s one-way ANOVA, with Student’s t-test as its two-group special case—a Monte Carlo study kept the Type I error within Bradley’s bounds in every condition examined: skewness up to 2, kurtosis up to 6, and group sizes from 5 to 100 [@Blanca:2017]. For unequal variances with two groups—Welch’s t-test—group sizes near 50 hold the 5% rate across a wide range of skewness, and only heavily skewed distributions call for substantially larger samples, on the order of 200 [@Fagerland:2012]. For unequal variances with more than two groups—Welch’s one-way ANOVA—about 50 observations per group suffice, except when more than four groups are compared under pronounced skew, where roughly 100 per group are required [@Delacre:2019].

Before manuscript use: (1) re-verify the Delacre page for the “\(\approx 100\) for \(k > 4\)” claim; (2) ensure @Blanca:2017 is in REFERENCES.bib (author-managed).
